analysis.one_liner: Forces the FCC to give the public months of notice, comment, and study before loosening media ownership rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in December 2007, never got a committee vote or floor action before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Communications Commission to publish any proposed change to its broadcast ownership rules in the Federal Register at least 90 days before a vote, then hold a 60-day public comment period and a 30-day reply period [S2][S3]. If the FCC skipped those steps, the change would be void [S3]. Before touching rules that let companies own a newspaper and a TV station in the same city, the FCC would have had to complete a separate rulemaking to promote local programming and study how station pairings and newspaper-TV cross-ownership affect local news quality, media jobs, and local culture [S2][S3]. It would also have created an independent panel on increasing women and minority ownership of broadcast stations, which the FCC would have to act on before changing ownership rules [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Communities that depend on local news would benefit: the bill was built to slow the wave of mergers that packs multiple stations and newspapers into single companies, which typically means fewer local newsrooms and jobs [S2][S3]. Women and minorities, who hold a small share of broadcast licenses, would gain an official panel with a required census of who owns stations and a study of how consolidation affects their chances of owning one [S3]. Anyone who wanted a real say in FCC media decisions would get guaranteed notice and comment windows instead of rushed end-of-year votes [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Local news audiences and underserved owners

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least 90 days of public notice, a 60-day comment period, and a 30-day reply period before the FCC votes on any broadcast ownership rule change, with the change void if the FCC skips these steps

Forces the FCC to complete a separate rulemaking promoting local programming and to study how TV duopolies and newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership affect the quantity and quality of local news, local media jobs, and local cultural programming before loosening those rules

Establishes an independent panel on women and minority broadcast ownership, backed by a full census of the race and gender of station owners, whose recommendations the FCC must act on before changing ownership rules
Applies these requirements retroactively to any ownership rule changes attempted after October 1, 2007

analysis.who_pays: Large broadcast and newspaper companies that want to buy more stations and combine newspapers with TV stations in the same market would bear the cost: each change they pursue would take many months longer, face public opposition on the record, and could be undone for procedural defects. The FCC itself would carry the workload of extra rulemakings, a market-level study of every change, and an ownership census.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big media owners and the FCC

drawbacks.text: The procedural requirements are heavy: a 90-day notice, 60-day comment, 30-day reply, a separate local-content rulemaking, and a market-level study before each ownership change could delay even well-founded rule changes for a year or more
The bill's trigger that voids any non-compliant ownership rule change could produce litigation over whether the FCC followed each step, tying up media policy in court
The bill addresses process and study rather than setting ownership limits itself, so a determined commission could still eventually loosen the rules after satisfying the requirements

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a public record, genuine comment periods, and hard data on what consolidation does to local news — are real but procedural; the bill does not itself stop a merger, it slows one down and forces the evidence into the open. The cost is slowness: media rules could take a year or more per change and invite litigation over compliance. For a field where the FCC had historically moved quickly, that delay is the point, but critics could fairly call it a procedural obstacle rather than a fix for media consolidation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its telecommunications subcommittee in December 2007, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Representative Jay Inslee introduced the Media Ownership Act of 2007 on December 18, 2007, joined by Republican Representative Dave Reichert, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet the same day
Thirteen members cosponsored the bill: 12 Democrats and 1 Republican
The bill's notice, comment, local-content, and ownership-diversity requirements would have applied to ownership rule changes attempted after October 1, 2007
No further action was taken after the initial referral, and the bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large media companies were better off: the FCC remained free to relax ownership rules on its own timetable, without the months of notice, comment, and study this bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large media companies and the FCC

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided: the bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Republican cosponsor, and 12 of its 13 cosponsors were Democrats.

industries.industry: Large broadcast station groups and newspaper chains
industries.note: The bill would have delayed and complicated every attempt to relax ownership limits, the rules that let these companies assemble multiple stations and newspaper-TV combinations in single markets. Consolidation of this kind has historically been associated with fewer separate local newsrooms, so the industry's interest in faster deregulation ran against the local-news interests the bill protected.

industries.industry: Women and minority broadcast ownership aspirants
industries.note: The bill would have created a census of who owns stations, a study of how concentration affects minority ownership, and an independent panel recommending rules to increase it. Fewer station owners competing for licenses has historically meant fewer opportunities for new entrants.

industries.industry: Local broadcast newsrooms and independent station owners
industries.note: By forcing a study of duopolies and cross-ownership before any loosening, and requiring a rulemaking to promote local programming, the bill would have slowed the consolidation that squeezes independent stations and local news jobs.
